DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The proposal raises the Friday and Saturday Best Available Rate (BAR) from £145 to £165 and adds a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday. It claims at least £204,000 a year, on the grounds that weekend guests aren't price-sensitive.

The direction is reasonable: the hotel is priced below its competitive set. But the revenue figure uses the wrong room count. The price-sensitivity evidence is confounded by seasonality. And the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday segment, wedding guests, so £204,000 is not a floor.

## 1. What checks out

- The 2025 weekend occupancy average is 79% (950 / 12 = 79.2).
- 104 weekend nights a year is 52 weeks × 2.
- The competitor gap is right: competitors charge £165–£180 against our £145, so we are £20–£35 below.
- The £204,000 arithmetic is internally correct: 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = £203,757. But see the next point about the room count.

## 2. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and overstates its base

- **Room count.** Section 2 says Harbourside has **112** rooms. Section 5 calculates on **124**. On 112 rooms the same calculation gives about **£184,000**.
- **Not every weekend room pays BAR.** The £20 applies only to rooms sold at BAR. Corporate rates, contracted group rates and wedding blocks (38% of Saturday bookings) don't move, so the true base is smaller.
- **Commission is ignored.** For rooms sold through online travel agencies (OTAs), commission of typically 15–18% takes a share of the £20. The paper doesn't show its channel mix, so the size of this deduction can't be checked.
- **First-year revenue will be lower.** Bookings already made for summer weekends at £145 will be honoured. Summer weekends are often booked well ahead, so a good share of June–August revenue won't see the increase.

A defensible first-year estimate is well below £184,000. Showing the share of weekend room-nights sold at BAR would settle it.

## 3. The price-sensitivity "test" can't separate price from season

- **The evidence.** The rate rose by £10 at the end of June 2025, and occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July.
- **Why it doesn't show insensitivity.** The paper itself says July and August are the strongest months, because of the harbour festival and school holidays. A rise in July would have happened at any price. The comparison that would isolate the price effect is July 2025 against July 2024, or the 2025 June-to-July change against previous years. The paper shows neither.
- **The increase being tested now is larger.** The 2025 rise was 7% (£135 to £145). This one is 14% (£145 to £165).
- **"Reinforced our positioning" is speculation.** Nothing in the data supports it.
- **The value-for-money score of 8.4 was earned at £145.** A high value score is partly a result of being cheaper than competitors. At £165 we would match the cheapest hotel in the set, and the score could fall.

**Break-even.** The rise is about 14%, so weekend volume can fall by about 12% (1 − 145/165) before room revenue drops. That is about 9.6 occupancy points from a 79% base. That margin is reasonable, but it is a margin of safety; it isn't evidence that guests are insensitive to price.

## 4. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

The paper's own data:
- weddings at Quayside Hall account for **38% of Saturday bookings**;
- wedding guests **arrive Saturday and leave Sunday**.

These guests are exactly the one-night Saturday stays the minimum would block. Only *already-contracted* group rates are protected. Future wedding blocks, and wedding guests booking individually, would face the restriction. They would mostly book a hotel that lets them stay one night rather than pay for a second.

**Other problems with the minimum:**
- **It isn't needed on most Saturdays.** The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays. On the other ~21, a two-night minimum turns away one-night guests for rooms that would otherwise sit empty. Standard practice is to apply minimum stays only on dates likely to sell out.
- **The Sunday nights it creates aren't priced in this proposal.** If Sunday is sold at the midweek rate, the extra nights may be worth less than expected.

So the author's description, that the estimate "puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights," isn't conservative. The minimum has an unquantified upside *and* a potentially large unquantified downside, and the downside falls on the hotel's largest Saturday segment.

## 5. "Prudent" assumes no loss of occupancy

The paper calls holding 79% occupancy "prudent." But assuming *no fall* in occupancy after a 14% price rise is the optimistic case. And as section 3 shows, the evidence offered doesn't rule out a fall. £204,000 (really ~£184,000 before the deductions in section 2) is the best case, not a floor.

## 6. Monitoring is mostly sound

- Weekly pick-up against the same weeks in 2025 is the right comparison, and it addresses the seasonality problem in section 3.
- A five-point trigger sits inside the ~9.6-point break-even, so it is set sensibly.
- Two refinements:
  - Monthly occupancy averages can hide shoulder-month weakness behind strong summer weekends. Report Saturdays and wedding dates separately.
  - Set a separate trigger for wedding-block pick-up, because that is where the minimum stay is most likely to cost bookings.

## How the author's description compares

| Author's claim | Holds? |
|---|---|
| Weekend occupancy rose after the 2025 rate rise | True, but confounded by the July peak; it isn't a price test |
| Value score of 8.4 supports the rise | It was measured at £145; may not hold at £165 |
| Rates £20–£35 below competitors | Yes, but £165 equals the cheapest competitor |
| £204,000 is a floor | No. Uses 124 rooms instead of 112, applies the rise to all rooms, ignores commission and existing bookings, and assumes no fall in occupancy |
| Two-night minimum only adds value | No. It conflicts with wedding guests, 38% of Saturday bookings |
| Corporate and group commitments protected | Only already-contracted ones; future wedding blocks aren't |
| Monitoring will catch a dip | Largely yes, with the refinements above |

## Recommendation

**Approve a weekend BAR increase, but restate the case.**
- Use 112 rooms and the share of weekend room-nights actually sold at BAR.
- Deduct OTA commission and allow for bookings already on the books.
- Show the 12% break-even.
- Replace the June-to-July "test" with year-on-year data.

**Narrow the two-night minimum.**
- Apply it only on Saturdays forecast to sell out.
- Exempt wedding blocks and Quayside Hall wedding dates, or price one-night Saturday stays at a premium rather than refusing them.

**Keep the monitoring plan,** with Saturdays and wedding pick-up reported separately.
